scenes.line1: Why do pros use journalctl first?
scenes.say: When a Linux box fails, why do pros reach for journalctl first? And how do you filter logs fast enough to impress in interviews?

scenes.label: journalctl
scenes.sub: Queries all logs from systemd-journald: kernel, boots, services, syslog.
scenes.say: Journalctl lets you search all your logs in one place: kernel, boot, services, and syslog. It's the go-to tool on modern Linux.

scenes.title: Common journalctl commands
scenes.say: You can follow live logs for a service, show only errors from this boot, or jump to the end of the previous boot to see why it crashed.
Logs have priorities from zero, emergency, to seven, debug. Use -p to filter. For example, -p err shows only errors and worse.

scenes.question: Why can't you see logs from before reboot?
scenes.right: The journal isn't persistent. Set Storage=persistent and restart systemd-journald.
scenes.say: Interview trap: If you can't see logs from before a crash, it's usually because the journal isn't persistent. Set Storage equals persistent and restart systemd-journald.
